newsitem.title: CHINA: HK Democrats to monitor, not challenge legislature.
newsitem.headline: HK Democrats to monitor, not challenge legislature.

text.p: Hong Kong's Democratic Party will not launch a formal legal challenge to the controversial Provisional Legislature but will monitor the assembly carefully, party leader Martin Lee said on Saturday.

Lee, head of the biggest party in the now-disbanded Legislative Council, said a newly-established "shadow caucus" would oversee the interim parliament and "keep it honest" by reporting any mis-step to Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa.
"If they do anything, make any decision or pass any law which is prejudicial to our people, we will tell...Mr Tung and Mr Tung will stop them," Lee told a news conference.

Lee spoke to reporters four days after leading a public protest about the scrapping of the elected Council, speaking out from its balcony minutes after Britain handed Hong Kong back to China as a Special Region.
He said Tung could stop the legislature from passing any laws that would hurt Hong Kong people because the Beijing-appointed body was simply a rubber-stamp legislature that implemented China's will.

"Effectively I don't believe this Provisional Legislature is ever going to say no to Mr Tung and that is why if the Provisional Legislature has any ideas that are bad for Hong Kong the administration can stop them," he said.
The Democrats have not yet informed Tung of the new shadow caucus but Lee said that he has in the past welcomed comments.
"A month ago we asked Tung whether his senior officials would actually have meetings with us whenever we asked for them and he said no problem," said Lee.
In direct elections, a British reform that angered China, the Democratic Party won a majority of seats in the Legislative Council, the lawmaking body under colonial rule.
At Beijing's insistence, the assembly was dissolved and replaced by the Provisional Legislature at midnight on June 30 following the handover of Hong Kong after more than 150 years of British rule.
The new legislature sparked controversy by enacting laws before the formal transfer of power.

Chief Executive Tung has said that fresh elections will be held by May 1998 but the Democrats maintain that the unelected legislature violates the Basic Law, Hong Kong's constitution, and should be replaced by an elected body now.
"Initially we were told (elections would take place) in 12 months and then 11 months and now 10 months, but it is still 10 months too late," said Lee.
But Lee said the Democrats would not mount a formal legal case against the Provisional Legislature because it expects other people to challenge its constitutionality.

"As long as the Provisional Legislature has passed any law, whether before or after July 1, any litigant...that is adversely affected by any law...is bound to challenge it and the constitutionality of the body that made the law," said Lee.
Lee said challenges to the legislature already have been made.
During the first court case tried in the new Hong Kong on Friday, barrister Paul Harris, a prominent human rights advocate, told the judge that the legal system was unconstitutional.
The Provisional Legislature will stage its first formal sitting in Hong Kong's Legislative Council building on Wednesday.

Lee, a prominent lawyer and human rights advocate who has wide backing from Western leaders, said he expected Hong Kong people to demonstrate against the session on Wednesday but that he would not take part.
"I do not plan to step back into the Legislative Council building until I am re-elected," he said.
